name: Space-Time Tradeoffs
intent: Treat memory and time as two budgets you can trade: precompute, cache and index to answer faster, or recompute, stream and sketch to use less memory, and count both costs before choosing, including the cost of building the structure.
scenario: A reporting service answers range-sum queries over an array of 1,000 numbers. Recomputing each sum costs 500 steps per query. A prefix-sum table brings a query down to 1 step for 1,001 cells of memory. A teammate proposes storing every possible range in an n x n table, which is fine at n = 1,000 and impossible at n = 100,000, where it needs 10 billion cells.
problem: Most speed-ups are paid for in memory, and most memory savings are paid for in time. Counting only one side leads to two classic failures: a fast algorithm that runs out of memory at production scale, and a memory-frugal one that recomputes the same thing forever. The build cost of a precomputed structure is easy to forget too: it only pays off if enough queries use it, and a cache with no limit eventually uses all the memory it was meant to save time with.

howItWorks.title: Spend memory to save time
howItWorks.text: Store something you would otherwise recompute: a lookup table, a cache of results, an index, memoized sub-answers, a hash set for membership tests, or prefix sums for range queries. A prefix-sum table of n + 1 totals turns a range sum from n/2 additions into one subtraction: 500 steps become 1 at n = 1,000, for 1,001 cells.

howItWorks.title: Pay the build cost, then count the break-even
howItWorks.text: The structure has to be built first: 1,000 steps for the prefix table, 1,000,000 for the full n x n table at n = 1,000. Total cost is build plus queries times per-query cost, so a precomputation only wins after enough queries: 3 for the prefix table, 2,005 for the full table. With only 2 queries, recomputing (1,000 steps) beats the prefix table (1,002). Estimate how many queries will really come.

howItWorks.title: Spend time to save memory
howItWorks.text: The opposite trade: recompute instead of storing, process a stream one item at a time instead of loading it all, work in place instead of copying, compress data and pay to decompress it, or use a probabilistic structure such as a Bloom filter (typically a few bits per item, with some false positives) instead of keeping every item. When the data does not fit in memory, this is the only direction available.

howItWorks.title: Measure space the way you measure time
howItWorks.text: Space complexity counts the extra memory an algorithm needs (auxiliary space) as a function of n, separately from the input itself. A recursion's call stack counts too: O(depth). An n x n table is O(n squared) cells: 10 billion at n = 100,000, about 80 GB if each cell takes 8 bytes, which is typical for a 64-bit number in a compact array. Objects, pointers and boxed values typically cost several times more per item, so the real figure is often larger than the cell count suggests.

howItWorks.title: Bound every cache, and mind the memory system
howItWorks.text: A cache with no eviction grows with the number of distinct keys: 41,834 entries after 100,000 requests in the sample, against 1,000 with a cap, which keeps memory bounded but gives up hits (58,166 hits uncapped, 2,169 capped with first-in-first-out on this random key stream). Separately, how data is laid out in memory can matter as much as operation counts: scanning an array in order is typically much faster than jumping between scattered objects, because processors fetch memory in blocks. That effect is machine-dependent, so measure before relying on it.

pros: Precomputation turns repeated expensive work into a lookup, often by orders of magnitude
Caches and indexes are general tools that apply far beyond range sums
Trading time for memory lets a job run at all on data that does not fit
Counting both budgets makes the choice explicit instead of accidental
cons: Extra memory can be the limit at scale, and quadratic tables hit it quickly
The structure must be built, and kept up to date if the data changes
A cache adds invalidation and eviction problems of its own
Saving memory by recomputing or sketching costs time or accuracy
whenToUse: The same expensive result is requested many times, so build cost is repaid
Queries are many and updates are rare, so a precomputed structure stays valid
Time matters and memory is plentiful, or the reverse, and you know which budget binds
whenNotToUse: A handful of queries: building the structure costs more than recomputing
A table whose size is quadratic or worse in an input that can be large
Data that changes constantly, so a precomputed structure is always stale
Memory-constrained environments, where the time saved is paid for in swapping or crashes
pitfalls: Counting only time: an n x n table is O(n squared) memory, and at n = 100,000 that is 10 billion cells, about 80 GB at 8 bytes each. Do the memory arithmetic before the design review
Ignoring the build cost: a table that costs 1,000,000 steps to fill and saves 499 steps per query needs about 2,005 queries to pay off; with 2 queries recomputing wins
A cache with no eviction or size limit in a long-running process: memory grows with every new key until the process is killed
Forgetting constant factors of memory: a list of boxed objects typically costs several times the raw 8 bytes per number, and every pointer adds to it; say 'typically' and measure
Assuming operation counts decide speed: memory access patterns (locality) can dominate, so an array scan and a pointer chase with equal operation counts can run at very different speeds
Precomputing something the queries never need: store only what the expected queries use, and prefer the smallest structure that gives the speed you need (a prefix table, not the full table)

roles.label: Query client
roles.description: Asks for the sum of a range, many times.

roles.label: Recompute path
roles.description: Adds up the range again for every query: no memory, many steps.

roles.label: Prefix-sum table
roles.description: n + 1 running totals, built once; a query is one subtraction.

roles.label: Full n x n table
roles.description: Every range pre-summed: one lookup, but quadratic memory.

roles.label: Memory budget
roles.description: The memory the machine really has.

quiz.question: A design stores the sum of every range of a 100,000-element array in an n x n table of 64-bit numbers. Roughly how much memory is that?
options: About 800 KB, because each query only needs to read one cell.
About 80 MB, since a table of 100,000 rows is a small table.
About 80 GB: 10 billion cells at 8 bytes each.
About 8 GB, because most ranges overlap and can share cells.
quiz.explanation: 100,000 x 100,000 = 10 billion cells, and at 8 bytes each that is about 80 GB: beyond most machines. A prefix-sum table answers the same queries with 100,001 cells. Always do the memory arithmetic, not only the time arithmetic.

quiz.question: With n = 1,000 and only 2 queries, which is cheaper in total steps: recomputing each sum (500 steps per query), or building a prefix-sum table first (1,000 build steps, 1 step per query)?
options: Recomputing: 1,000 steps against 1,002, since the build is not repaid by 2 queries.
The prefix table: it always wins because a query costs 1 step, however few there are.
They tie, since both end up reading the whole array once for the first query.
The prefix table: its memory use is tiny, so the build cost can be ignored.
quiz.explanation: Total cost is build plus queries times per-query cost. The prefix table costs 1,000 + 2 = 1,002 steps; recomputing costs 2 x 500 = 1,000. The prefix table pays off from 3 queries onwards.

quiz.question: A service caches results in a map with no size limit, and its keys come from user input. What happens over weeks of uptime?
options: Nothing, because a cache only stores values that were requested often.
The cache stops growing once it reaches the size of the database.
Old entries are removed automatically, since a map evicts what it has not read.
Memory grows with the number of distinct keys, until the process slows or is killed.
quiz.explanation: A plain map keeps every key it has ever stored: 41,834 entries after 100,000 requests in the sample. Give a cache a size cap and an eviction rule, and accept that some hits are lost (2,169 hits with a cap of 1,000, against 58,166 with no limit).
